chunks.label: Where you're from
chunks.rationale: Ask where someone is from and say where you grew up.
chunks.interference: doko kara kita no can also mean 'where have you just come from' today.

chunks.label: What you do for work
chunks.rationale: Ask about someone's job and describe your own.
chunks.interference: de hataraiteru takes de for the workplace, while sunderu takes ni.

chunks.label: Where you live now
chunks.rationale: Ask where someone lives and say how and where you live.
chunks.interference: jikka is your parents' home, not just any house you live in.

chunks.label: Why you came to Japan
chunks.rationale: Answer and ask the 'why Japan' question and what sparked it.
chunks.interference: nande asks for the reason; kikkake asks what set it off.

chunks.label: How long you're here
chunks.rationale: Say how long you've been in Japan and how long you'll stay.
chunks.interference: dono gurai looks back (how long so far); itsu made looks ahead (until when).

chunks.label: Speaking in Japanese
chunks.rationale: Say you're learning and steer the chat into Japanese.
chunks.interference: hanaseru? (can you speak) vs hanasou (let's speak).

chunks.label: Compliments on your Japanese
chunks.rationale: Handle the inevitable 'your Japanese is good' and the questions that follow.
chunks.interference: dokugaku (self-taught) sounds close to daigaku (university).

chunks.label: Meeting a friend's friend
chunks.rationale: Greet someone new through a mutual friend and swap contacts.
chunks.interference: rain here is the LINE app, not the weather.

chunks.label: Describing your hometown
chunks.rationale: Pin down where their hometown is and say what yours is like.
chunks.interference: dono hen (whereabouts) vs donna (what kind of).

chunks.label: Life in Japan
chunks.rationale: Answer how you're finding Japan and what you like about it.
chunks.interference: None.

chunks.label: Brothers sisters and family
chunks.rationale: Ask about siblings and family size and describe your own.
chunks.interference: ani is your own older brother; theirs is oniisan.

chunks.label: Studies and job hunting
chunks.rationale: Talk about what you study or that you're between jobs.
chunks.interference: ryuugaku (study abroad) vs ryokou (travel).

chunks.label: Age and birth year
chunks.rationale: Work out ages, which Japanese friends often check early.
chunks.interference: nannen umare (what year born) vs nannen (how many years).

chunks.label: Partner kids and pets
chunks.rationale: Ask about someone's household beyond their parents and siblings.
chunks.interference: katteru here means keeping a pet (飼う), not buying (買う).

chunks.label: Polite first-meeting questions
chunks.rationale: Recognise the formal versions people use with a stranger.
chunks.interference: These are polite forms; among friends doko kara kita no replaces dochira kara desu ka.

chunks.label: Hobbies and what you like
chunks.rationale: Ask about hobbies and say what you're into.
chunks.interference: no ga suki follows a verb (taberu no ga suki); a noun takes ga suki directly.

chunks.label: Weekends and free time
chunks.rationale: Say what you usually do when you're off.
chunks.interference: daitai (usually) vs zettai (definitely).

chunks.label: Do you do this
chunks.rationale: Ask about everyday pastimes with a simple yes-no question.
chunks.interference: jimu ni kayotteru (go regularly) vs jimu ni itta (went once).

chunks.label: Food you like
chunks.rationale: Trade favourite foods and say how adventurous you are.
chunks.interference: tabeta koto aru? (ever eaten it) vs tabeta? (did you eat).

chunks.label: Places you've been
chunks.rationale: Ask where someone has travelled and say where you want to go.
chunks.interference: itta koto aru? (ever been) vs itta? (did you go).

chunks.label: Shows and favourites
chunks.rationale: Swap what you've been watching and who you're a fan of.
chunks.interference: oshi is the person you're a fan of, not a crush.

chunks.label: Music and gigs
chunks.rationale: Ask about someone's music taste, gigs and karaoke songs.
chunks.interference: raibu is a live gig or concert, not 'live' as in living.

chunks.label: How long and how good
chunks.rationale: Follow up on a hobby by asking how long, and say how new or rusty you are.
chunks.interference: mukashi yatteta (used to do) vs yatteru (do now).

chunks.label: Getting into their hobby
chunks.rationale: Show interest in trying their hobby or pull them into yours.
chunks.interference: yatte mitai means want to try, not want to see.

chunks.label: Eating and drinking out
chunks.rationale: Sort out food and drink limits when you go out together.
chunks.interference: osake yowai means you get drunk easily, not that you dislike drinking.

chunks.label: Which type are you
chunks.rationale: Play the 'this or that' game about what kind of person you are.
chunks.interference: ha here means side or camp (派), not the topic particle wa.

chunks.label: Asking their view
chunks.rationale: Invite someone's opinion or reaction on a topic.
chunks.interference: sou omowanai? fishes for agreement; dou omou? is open.

chunks.label: Saying it's good
chunks.rationale: Give a quick positive verdict on something.
chunks.interference: omoshirokatta means fun or interesting, not only funny.

chunks.label: Saying it's not great
chunks.rationale: Give a mild negative verdict without sounding harsh.
chunks.interference: awanakatta (didn't suit me) vs aenakatta (couldn't meet).

chunks.label: Liking it your way
chunks.rationale: Say you like something in a low-key way and say what you like about it.
chunks.interference: warukunai and kirai ja nai sound negative but mean you like it.

chunks.label: Framing your own view
chunks.rationale: Open your opinion so it lands as personal, not as fact.
chunks.interference: watashi dattara (if it were me) vs watashi datta (it was me).

chunks.label: Comparing here and there
chunks.rationale: Compare Japan with home, or one thing with another.
chunks.interference: sumiyasui is easy (yasui) to live in, not cheap.

chunks.label: It depends
chunks.rationale: Avoid a flat answer when the honest view is 'it depends'.
chunks.interference: ichigai ni wa ienai (can't generalise) vs nantomo ienai (can't say).

chunks.label: Tastes differ
chunks.rationale: Say that opinions split without saying anyone is wrong.
chunks.interference: wakareru (split, divide) vs wakaru (understand).

chunks.label: Picking a side
chunks.rationale: Ask which option someone prefers and lean one way yourself.
chunks.interference: dotchi? (which one) vs dotchika (either one); ha is 'camp' (派), not the particle wa.

chunks.label: Rating words
chunks.rationale: Shade a verdict up or down with a small degree word.
chunks.interference: futsuu ni can mean 'honestly, really', not just 'normally'.

chunks.label: Kind of like
chunks.rationale: Describe something by likeness when you lack the exact word.
chunks.interference: trailing mitai na ('like, ...') vs mitai (want to see).

chunks.label: Weighing their point
chunks.rationale: Acknowledge someone's view before adding your own.
chunks.interference: iitai koto wa wakaru signals a 'but' is coming, not full agreement.

chunks.label: Impressions and stereotypes
chunks.rationale: Share an impression or doubt while flagging it may be unfair.
chunks.interference: imeeji means impression, not picture.

chunks.label: Shrugging it off
chunks.rationale: Let a point go or play something down.
chunks.interference: saa can mean 'who knows' or 'come on, let's go'.

chunks.label: Sounding unimpressed
chunks.rationale: Recognise or voice a cool, dismissive take.
chunks.interference: dou demo ii (don't care) sounds cold; nandemo ii (anything's fine) is the friendly one.

chunks.label: How have you been
chunks.rationale: Open a catch-up by asking how someone's doing.
chunks.interference: genki datta? (been well since we last met) vs genki? (are you well).

chunks.label: Nothing much new
chunks.rationale: Answer 'how are you' when life is just ticking along.
chunks.interference: kawari nai (nothing's changed) vs kawaranai (won't change).

chunks.label: Busy tired or rested
chunks.rationale: Say how busy or worn out you've been.
chunks.interference: nebusoku (short on sleep) vs nemui (sleepy right now).

chunks.label: Last weekend
chunks.rationale: Ask about and sum up a weekend or holiday.
chunks.interference: yukkuri dekita (got to relax) vs yukkuri (slowly).

chunks.label: How work is going
chunks.rationale: Check in on someone's job, the default catch-up topic.
chunks.interference: shigoto nani shiteru no asks what job; shigoto dou asks how it's going.

chunks.label: Your news
chunks.rationale: Share what's new with you and follow up on their news.
chunks.interference: hamatteru (hooked on) vs haitteru (is inside).

chunks.label: Weather and seasons
chunks.rationale: Make the easy seasonal small talk Japanese conversations open with.
chunks.interference: mushiatsui (humid) vs atsui (hot).

chunks.label: Days off and plans
chunks.rationale: Ask about days off and say you've got nothing on.
chunks.interference: yotei (plans) vs yoyaku (booking).

chunks.label: Seeing someone again
chunks.rationale: Greet a friend you haven't seen in a long time.
chunks.interference: nannenburi (how many years) vs hisashiburi (long time no see).

chunks.label: Asking about their people
chunks.rationale: Ask after someone's family, partner or a mutual friend.
chunks.interference: dou shiteru (how are they doing) vs dou shita (what happened).

chunks.label: Casual check-in texts
chunks.rationale: Send or answer the light check-ins friends drop by message.
chunks.interference: gohan tabeta? is a caring check-in, not an invitation to eat.

chunks.label: Noticing changes
chunks.rationale: Comment on a new haircut or look, or on your own weight.
chunks.interference: kitta (cut) vs kita (came, wore).

chunks.label: Time flies
chunks.rationale: Remark on how fast the year goes and ask about holiday plans.
chunks.interference: kaeru (go home) sounds the same as kaeru (change).

chunks.label: Polite small talk
chunks.rationale: Handle formal small talk with older people or acquaintances.
chunks.interference: desu ne is polite; with friends it drops to atsui ne.

chunks.label: Uh-huh I'm listening
chunks.rationale: Shows you're following while your friend talks.
chunks.interference: fuun can sound bored if overused, and hai-hai can sound dismissive.

chunks.label: Really seriously
chunks.rationale: Reacts with surprise to news so the teller keeps going.
chunks.interference: ee needs a rising pitch or it sounds like a polite 'yes'; uso desho isn't calling them a liar.

chunks.label: Oh I didn't know
chunks.rationale: Acknowledges new information or a sudden understanding.
chunks.interference: sou datta n da takes in news; sou iu koto ka means it finally clicked.

chunks.label: So true so relatable
chunks.rationale: Signals you share the feeling or experience they describe.
chunks.interference: aru aru means 'that happens', wakaru wakaru means 'I feel that'.

chunks.label: Sounds fun looks good
chunks.rationale: Comments on what someone describes, shows or serves you.
chunks.interference: -sou guesses from outside; oishisou is before eating, oishikatta after.

chunks.label: Good for you
chunks.rationale: Responds warmly when a friend shares good news.
chunks.interference: ii naa is envy for them, ii jan is approval; yokatta ne is for them, yokatta alone is your own relief.

chunks.label: No way unbelievable
chunks.rationale: Reacts strongly to something shocking or outrageous.
chunks.interference: iya iya also brushes off compliments; arienai can mean outrageous, not just surprising.

chunks.label: What you're kidding
chunks.rationale: Challenges something odd or cheeky someone just said.
chunks.interference: nani sore can sound scornful; uso tsuke is playful only with close friends.

chunks.label: Wow and whoa
chunks.rationale: Gives a quick gut reaction to something you see or hear.
chunks.interference: uwa can be delight or disgust; ara sounds older or feminine.

chunks.label: Well done never mind
chunks.rationale: Responds to how someone did, whether they nailed it or missed.
chunks.interference: yatta ne is 'you did it', yatta is 'I did it'; yoku yatta can sound top-down.

chunks.label: Yes I did it
chunks.rationale: Celebrates your own win or a bit of luck.
chunks.interference: yossha sounds masculine; dekita also means 'it's ready'.

chunks.label: Oh that's all
chunks.rationale: Reacts when the story or news turns out smaller than expected.
chunks.interference: naanda can be relief or letdown; haa? with a rising tone sounds rude.

chunks.label: Huh that's odd
chunks.rationale: Voices puzzlement at something strange.
chunks.interference: nani kore is about a thing in front of you, nani sore about what they said.

chunks.label: Oops oh no
chunks.rationale: Reacts to small mistakes and mishaps.
chunks.interference: shimatta is your own slip; arara reacts to anyone's small mishap.

chunks.label: Ugh damn ouch
chunks.rationale: Lets out frustration or pain.
chunks.interference: kuso and chikushou are rough; mou is mild annoyance.

chunks.label: Doing things together
chunks.rationale: Covers the little noises of handling things side by side.
chunks.interference: kore kore can also scold ('now, now'); seeno times a group action.

chunks.label: And then what
chunks.rationale: Pushes a story forward to the next part.
chunks.interference: A flat sore de? sounds impatient; nani nani is eager, not suspicious.

chunks.label: How was it
chunks.rationale: Gets someone talking about an event, trip or weekend.
chunks.interference: dou datta asks about the past; dou is about now.

chunks.label: And you your take
chunks.rationale: Turns the question back and draws out their preferences and views.
chunks.interference: sotchi wa is the casual 'you'; anata wa sounds cold.

chunks.label: What's it like
chunks.rationale: Asks how a job, place or new situation is going.
chunks.interference: tte dou attaches to a noun ('shigoto tte dou?'); donna kanji stands alone.

chunks.label: Asking about people
chunks.rationale: Finds out about the people in someone's life and story.
chunks.interference: nante itteta asks what they said; nante iu asks what something is called.

chunks.label: What's new with you
chunks.rationale: Catches up on what a friend has been up to.
chunks.interference: nanika atta asks if something's wrong; nanka ii koto atta asks about something good.

chunks.label: Since when who told
chunks.rationale: Digs into the details behind a piece of news or gossip.
chunks.interference: nande shitteru no can sound accusing without a smile.

chunks.label: Asking first asking advice
chunks.rationale: Opens a question, checks it's okay, or asks for advice.
chunks.interference: ii no? checks it's really okay; ii yo is the reply 'it's fine'.

chunks.label: Yes exactly
chunks.rationale: Agrees warmly with what your friend just said.
chunks.interference: sou sou confirms their point; da yo ne echoes a shared feeling.

chunks.label: Me too I agree
chunks.rationale: Says you share their view or experience.
chunks.interference: 'me neither' is watashi mo + a negative verb, not watashi mo alone; sono toori is a bit formal.

chunks.label: OK got it
chunks.rationale: Accepts a suggestion or confirms you understood.
chunks.interference: wakarimashita is polite; ryoukai can sound curt to elders.

chunks.label: Hmm I'm not sure
chunks.rationale: Hedges instead of fully agreeing.
chunks.interference: uun can mean 'no' or just 'hmm' depending on pitch; maa ne is half agreement, not a yes.

chunks.label: Not really
chunks.rationale: Disagrees gently by playing the claim down.
chunks.interference: sou demo nai means 'not really'; sou ja nai means 'that's wrong'.

chunks.label: True but
chunks.rationale: Grants their point before pushing back.
chunks.interference: The trailing kedo does the disagreeing; there's no need to add demo.

chunks.label: Fair point
chunks.rationale: Concedes a good point in a discussion.
chunks.interference: sore wa aru means 'that's a factor'; aru aru means 'so relatable'.

chunks.label: I don't think so
chunks.rationale: Disagrees firmly or corrects a claim.
chunks.interference: sore wa nai rejects an idea, not a person; chigau chigau corrects a fact.

chunks.label: Didn't catch that
chunks.rationale: Asks for a repeat or slower speech when you're lost.
chunks.interference: The kudasai and onegai shimasu forms are polite; wakarimasen can mean 'I don't know'.

chunks.label: What do you mean
chunks.rationale: Asks what or who they are referring to.
chunks.interference: nan no hanashi? can sound like denial if said sharply.

chunks.label: What's the word
chunks.rationale: Buys time when a word escapes you.
chunks.interference: nan dakke recalls a thing, nante iu n dakke recalls a word; both are half to yourself.

chunks.label: No I mean
chunks.rationale: Corrects yourself or takes something back.
chunks.interference: sou ja nakute fixes your own words; chotto chigau kana gently fixes theirs.

chunks.label: Did I get it
chunks.rationale: Checks you understood or were understood.
chunks.interference: atteru asks if you're right; kikoeru is for bad audio or calls.

chunks.label: Hey guess what
chunks.rationale: Grabs attention to start a story or share news.
chunks.interference: ano ne and ano sa open a topic; a drawn-out ano... is just hesitation.

chunks.label: By the way
chunks.rationale: Shifts to a new topic or back to an old one.
chunks.interference: hanashi kawaru changes the topic; hanashi modoru goes back.

chunks.label: Wrapping up
chunks.rationale: Ends a chat or call smoothly.
chunks.interference: jaa sou iu koto de settles a plan rather than just saying goodbye.

chunks.label: Managing a long story
chunks.rationale: Hands the turn over, takes it back, and keeps a long story on track.
chunks.interference: kke marks trying to recall (doko made hanashita kke), not a plain question.

chunks.label: Got a minute
chunks.rationale: Opens a request, a serious talk, or a call for attention.
chunks.interference: chotto hanashi ga aru can sound ominous; nanka you? is blunt.

chunks.label: Moving the story along
chunks.rationale: Lets you carry a story forward and signal a twist is coming.
chunks.interference: sore de sa just moves on, while sore ga sa warns that a twist is coming.

chunks.label: Getting to the point
chunks.rationale: Lets you sum up, give the reason, or reveal what really happened.
chunks.interference: honto wa (the truth is) is easy to mix up with the reaction honto? (really?).

chunks.label: Opening a story
chunks.rationale: Lets you launch into a story or hook the listener before you start.
chunks.interference: mou ittakke? (did I tell you?) is easy to confuse with mou itta (I already said it).

chunks.label: Own little slip-ups
chunks.rationale: Lets you own up to small everyday mistakes when you tell what happened.
chunks.interference: The -chatta endings blur together, and tsui ... shichatta needs a verb in the gap.

chunks.label: Hazy memory and hindsight
chunks.rationale: Lets you hedge details you are not sure of and look back on events.
chunks.interference: tashika (if I remember right) is not tashikani (certainly; true).

chunks.label: Framing a story
chunks.rationale: Lets you play a story down or mark it as an aside or a secret.
chunks.interference: betsu ni ii n da kedo softens the start, but betsu ni alone sounds curt.

chunks.label: Things gone wrong
chunks.rationale: Lets you report a lost, broken or missed thing in a story.
chunks.interference: nakushita (lost it) and wasureta (forgot it) get swapped, as do kowareta (broke) and ugokanai (won't run).

chunks.label: Sympathy for a hard time
chunks.rationale: Lets you show you understand when someone tells you something rough.
chunks.interference: taihen datta ne is for something over, taihen da ne for something still going; kawaisou ni can sound condescending.

chunks.label: Telling them not to worry
chunks.rationale: Lets you wave off an apology or settle someone's worry.
chunks.interference: ki ni shinaide (never mind it) and shinpai shinaide (don't worry) overlap, while zenzen daijoubu is about yourself.

chunks.label: Saying you are worn out
chunks.rationale: Lets you say how tired you are when someone asks how you are.
chunks.interference: nemurenakatta (couldn't sleep) is not nemui (sleepy).

chunks.label: Hungry and thirsty
chunks.rationale: Lets you say you need food or a drink.
chunks.interference: hara hetta is rough and masculine; onaka suita is the neutral one.

chunks.label: Had enough
chunks.rationale: Lets you vent that you are fed up or have reached your limit.
chunks.interference: The mou set starts alike: muri (can't), yada (hate it), dame (hopeless), ii (forget it); hottoite is harsh.

chunks.label: Checking on someone
chunks.rationale: Lets you ask if a friend is okay or doing better.
chunks.interference: daijoubu desu ka is polite; with friends just daijoubu? is enough.

chunks.label: Oh no moments
chunks.rationale: Lets you voice panic, nerves or being stuck.
chunks.interference: dou shiyou (what do I do?) is not dou suru? (what shall we do?).

chunks.label: Feeling relieved
chunks.rationale: Lets you say the worry is over.
chunks.interference: anshin shita and hotto shita are near-synonyms, and raku ni natta also means it got easier.

chunks.label: Low moods
chunks.rationale: Lets you say you are down, torn or unmotivated.
chunks.interference: ochikonderu (feeling down) and nayanderu (torn, worrying over something) get swapped.

chunks.label: Easing someone up
chunks.rationale: Lets you tell someone to relax, slow down or stop overthinking.
chunks.interference: yukkuri de ii yo and aseranakute ii yo mean the same, and ochitsuite can sound like a scolding.

chunks.label: Too much food or drink
chunks.rationale: Lets you say you are full, stuffed or drunk.
chunks.interference: tabesugita and nomisugita differ by one verb, and onaka ippai (full) is not mou ippai (one more).

chunks.label: Being moved
chunks.rationale: Lets you say a show, song or moment got to you.
chunks.interference: nakeru (it makes you cry) is not naku (to cry), and tereru is about your own blushing.

chunks.label: Cheering someone on
chunks.rationale: Lets you encourage effort and praise it afterwards.
chunks.interference: yoku ganbatta ne is for effort already made, faito for effort ahead.

chunks.label: Feeling refreshed
chunks.rationale: Lets you say something left you feeling better or revived.
chunks.interference: sukkiri (clear, unburdened) and sappari (clean, fresh) sound alike.

chunks.label: Get well wishes
chunks.rationale: Lets you wish a sick friend a quick recovery.
chunks.interference: odaiji ni is only for illness or injury, not a general take care.

chunks.label: Comforting someone upset
chunks.rationale: Lets you comfort a friend who is down or in tears.
chunks.interference: yoshi yoshi is for kids and pets and can sound patronising to an adult.

chunks.label: Inviting someone out
chunks.rationale: Lets you invite a friend to eat, drink or come along.
chunks.interference: The -nai? ending is an invitation, not "aren't you going?".

chunks.label: Finding a time and place
chunks.rationale: Lets you check if someone is free and pin down when and where.
chunks.interference: aiteru? (are you free?) is easy to mix up with aite (partner).

chunks.label: Saying yes to plans
chunks.rationale: Lets you accept an invite with enthusiasm.
chunks.interference: tsukiau (keep you company) also means to date someone.

chunks.label: Turning down softly
chunks.rationale: Lets you say no to an invite without bluntness.
chunks.interference: kyou wa chotto works because it trails off, so don't finish the sentence.

chunks.label: Deciding what to do
chunks.rationale: Lets you ask what to do and show you are easy either way.
chunks.interference: dou suru? (what shall we do?) is not dou shiyou (what do I do?!).

chunks.label: Settling the plan
chunks.rationale: Lets you agree on a choice and lock it in.
chunks.interference: sou shiyou (let's do that) and sou suru (I'll do that) differ in who acts.

chunks.label: On the way
chunks.rationale: Lets you check where someone is and report where you are.
chunks.interference: tsuita (I've arrived) and tsuku (I will arrive) get swapped.

chunks.label: Maybe next time
chunks.rationale: Lets you leave the door open when you can't or won't commit.
chunks.interference: mata kondo can be a polite no rather than a real promise.

chunks.label: Delays and call-backs
chunks.rationale: Lets you handle running late, dropping out, or calling later.
chunks.interference: ato de denwa suru (I'll call) and ato de kakenaosu (I'll call back) overlap.

chunks.label: End of the night
chunks.rationale: Lets you suggest leaving, offer a ride home, or order one more.
chunks.interference: mou ippai (one more drink) is not onaka ippai (I'm full).

chunks.label: Joking around
chunks.rationale: Lets you mark a joke, ask for the punchline, or admit one bombed.
chunks.interference: uso uso (just kidding) is not the reaction uso! (no way!).

chunks.label: Laughing it off
chunks.rationale: Lets you deny or shrug off teasing.
chunks.interference: sore ga nanika? (so what?) can sound combative if said flat.

chunks.label: Stop teasing me
chunks.rationale: Lets you ask someone to ease off when they tease you.
chunks.interference: yamete can sound truly upset, so tone carries the playfulness.

chunks.label: Told you so
chunks.rationale: Lets you gloat when you were right or a habit repeats.
chunks.interference: hora ne (see? told you) is not hora (look!).

chunks.label: Calling out bragging
chunks.rationale: Lets you poke fun at someone showing off.
chunks.interference: yoku iu (look who's talking) uses the same words as yoku iu (often say).

chunks.label: Spoilers and killjoys
chunks.rationale: Lets you handle someone spoiling the fun or the mood.
chunks.interference: nori warui (no fun) has nothing to do with noru meaning to ride.

chunks.label: Hey, cut that out
chunks.rationale: Lets you recognise rough calls to stop or pay attention.
chunks.interference: These are mostly for hearing; kora and iikagen ni shiro sound like scolding.

chunks.label: Rough comebacks
chunks.rationale: Lets you recognise harsh retorts and how hard they hit.
chunks.interference: baka ja nai no can be fond or cutting depending on tone, and shiru ka is ruder than shiranai.

chunks.label: Bye for now
chunks.rationale: Lets you say goodbye to a friend you will see again soon.
chunks.interference: sayounara sounds final; mata ne is the friendly default.

chunks.label: Saying hi
chunks.rationale: Lets you greet a friend or someone you run into.
chunks.interference: doumo means both hi and thanks.

chunks.label: Thanking a friend
chunks.rationale: Lets you thank someone casually for a favour.
chunks.interference: warui ne here means thanks, I owe you, not "that's bad".

chunks.label: Saying sorry
chunks.rationale: Lets you apologise to a friend, lightly or properly.
chunks.interference: gomen gomen is light, and suman is masculine.

chunks.label: Ending a hangout
chunks.rationale: Lets you wrap up time together warmly and stay in touch.
chunks.interference: tsuitara rain shite (text me when you get home) and rain shite (message me) differ only by the first word.

chunks.label: Replying to thanks
chunks.rationale: Lets you brush off thanks or praise.
chunks.interference: douitashimashite sounds stiff between friends; ie ie is the natural reply.

chunks.label: What to call each other
chunks.rationale: Lets you settle names and casual speech when you first meet.
chunks.interference: ... tte yonde (call me ...) is not yonde (read it).

chunks.label: Late or out of touch
chunks.rationale: Lets you apologise for keeping someone waiting or going quiet.
chunks.interference: matta? (did you wait?) is not matte (wait).

chunks.label: At the table
chunks.rationale: Lets you toast, treat, and call people to eat.
chunks.interference: ogoru (to treat) and okoru (to get angry) sound close.

chunks.label: Asking a favour
chunks.rationale: Lets you ask a friend for help or for something.
chunks.interference: choudai (give me) gets mixed up with chotto (a bit).

chunks.label: Take care wishes
chunks.rationale: Lets you wish someone well when you part.
chunks.interference: ki o tsukete (take care) gets mixed up with ki ni shinaide (don't worry).

chunks.label: Offering help
chunks.rationale: Lets you offer a hand and thank someone for theirs.
chunks.interference: tetsudaou ka (shall I help?) is not tetsudatte (help me).

chunks.label: Heading off
chunks.rationale: Lets you leave before others or part for longer.
chunks.interference: osaki ni (I'm off first) is not osaki ni douzo (after you).

chunks.label: Congratulations
chunks.rationale: Lets you congratulate a friend on a milestone.
chunks.interference: omedetou and arigatou both end in -ou and can slip.

chunks.label: Visiting a home
chunks.rationale: Lets you enter and leave a friend's place politely.
chunks.interference: ojama shimasu is for arriving, ojama shimashita for leaving.

chunks.label: Go ahead and help yourself
chunks.rationale: Lets you put a guest or friend at ease.
chunks.interference: enryo shinaide (don't hold back) is not enryo shite okimasu (I'll pass).

chunks.label: Replying to kindness
chunks.rationale: Lets you accept or politely decline someone's fuss over you.
chunks.interference: enryo naku accepts, while okamai naku declines.

chunks.label: Thanks for everything
chunks.rationale: Lets you thank someone at the end of work, a stay or a stretch of time.
chunks.interference: otsukaresama deshita thanks effort and does not mean "you are tired".

chunks.label: Leaving and coming home
chunks.rationale: Lets you use the set phrases at the door of a shared home.
chunks.interference: tadaima is said by the one arriving, okaeri by the one at home.

chunks.label: Begging a favour
chunks.rationale: Lets you plead hard for help or forgiveness.
chunks.interference: tanomu kara and onegai dakara mean the same, and both are stronger than tanomu yo.

chunks.label: Polite apologies
chunks.rationale: Lets you apologise formally to someone outside your circle.
chunks.interference: doumo sumimasen can also mean thank you so much.

chunks.label: Holiday greetings
chunks.rationale: Lets you greet friends at Christmas and New Year.
chunks.interference: yoi otoshi o is said before New Year, akemashite omedetou only after.

chunks.label: Asking and declining politely
chunks.rationale: Ask if something is okay, offer something, ask a favour or turn an offer down in any polite setting.
chunks.interference: Kekkou desu usually means no thanks rather than great, and yoroshii desu ka is just a politer ii desu ka.

chunks.label: Eating out with friends
chunks.rationale: Get a meal or drinks with friends going, from the first beer to splitting the bill.
chunks.interference: Okawari (a refill) and okaikei (the bill) both start with o-ka and get swapped.

chunks.label: Ordering food
chunks.rationale: Pick dishes, ask what's good, get water and say you're done ordering.
chunks.interference: Ijou desu (that's all) is easy to mix with ii desu (no thanks).

chunks.label: Table or takeaway
chunks.rationale: Say how many you are, whether you're eating in or taking it away, and ask for a bigger portion.
chunks.interference: Tennai de (eat in) and mochikaeri de (take away) are easy to swap.

chunks.label: Paying at the till
chunks.rationale: Ask the price, check card and tax, and get a receipt when you pay.
chunks.interference: Ryoushuusho is the formal receipt for expenses, not the till slip reshiito.

chunks.label: Finding your way
chunks.rationale: Ask for the toilet or directions, say you're lost, and tell a driver or crowd where you're getting off.
chunks.interference: Koko doko (where am I?) sounds close to koko de ii desu (here is fine), and orimasu is also the humble word for 'to be' at work.

chunks.label: Emergencies
chunks.rationale: Shout about an earthquake, say where it hurts and call for help or an ambulance.
chunks.interference: None.

chunks.label: Just browsing
chunks.rationale: Keep shop staff at bay, try things on and leave without buying.
chunks.interference: Chotto kangaemasu and ato de mata kimasu both usually mean no sale, not a real promise to come back.

chunks.label: Bags and wrapping
chunks.rationale: Accept or refuse a bag or receipt and say whether it needs gift wrapping.
chunks.interference: Daijoubu desu here means no thanks, so fukuro wa daijoubu desu turns the bag down.

chunks.label: Around the office
chunks.rationale: Greet coworkers, head home before others and come back from going out.
chunks.interference: Gokurousama goes to juniors or workers, so saying it to a senior instead of otsukaresama is rude.

chunks.label: Staff making you wait
chunks.rationale: Understand staff saying certainly, one moment, coming, and here you are.
chunks.interference: Tadaima ukagaimasu (coming right away) is not tadaima, I'm home.

chunks.label: Staff greetings
chunks.rationale: Recognise the welcome, take your time and come again lines staff say as you arrive and leave.
chunks.interference: Omachi shite orimashita (we were expecting you) gets mixed with omatase shimashita (sorry to keep you waiting).

chunks.label: Getting seated
chunks.rationale: Answer the questions and directions staff give as they seat you.
chunks.interference: Kochira e douzo (this way) is easy to confuse with kochira no reji e douzo (this register).

chunks.label: Staff taking your order
chunks.rationale: Follow the waiter asking if you're ready, what you'll drink, whether that's all and if they can clear plates.
chunks.interference: The two gochuumon questions differ only at the end: okimari (ready to order?) versus ijou de yoroshii (is that all?).

chunks.label: Convenience store questions
chunks.rationale: Answer the cashier's quick questions about heating, bags, chopsticks and points cards.
chunks.interference: Otsuke shimasu ka (shall I add one?) is easy to confuse with omochi desu ka (do you have one?).

chunks.label: Staff taking payment
chunks.rationale: Follow the cashier through payment method, money handed over, change and one bill or one payment.
chunks.interference: Goissho (one bill for the group) and ikkatsu (one card payment, no instalments) both sound like 'all at once'.

chunks.label: At the counter
chunks.rationale: Respond when you're called up to the counter and asked if it's for here or to go.
chunks.interference: Omeshiagari (eating, honorific) hides the plain tennai de you answer with.

chunks.label: Shop staff approaching
chunks.rationale: Recognise staff offering help or inviting you to look, so you can answer with miteru dake desu.
chunks.interference: Nanika osagashi (looking for something?) and nanika goyou (need anything?) are near twins.

chunks.label: Formal replies at work
chunks.rationale: Answer a request or instruction at work with understood, I'll check, I'll consider it or you're right.
chunks.interference: Kentou shimasu often means a polite no, unlike kakunin shimasu, which promises a real check.

chunks.label: Asking favours formally
chunks.rationale: Open and soften a request to someone senior or a stranger in a formal setting.
chunks.interference: Osoreirimasu works as both thanks and excuse me, much like sumimasen.

chunks.label: Formal apologies
chunks.rationale: Apologise seriously at work or to a customer for a mistake or trouble caused.
chunks.interference: Moushiwake arimasen and gozaimasen are the same apology; gozaimasen is the politer staff form.

chunks.label: Business phone calls
chunks.rationale: Open a business call, ask who's calling and promise to call back.
chunks.interference: Orikaeshi (call back) sounds like okaeshi (your change).

chunks.label: At the clinic desk
chunks.rationale: Follow reception at a clinic or office asking what's wrong, your name and your insurance card.
chunks.interference: Okake kudasai (have a seat) is easy to mix with omachi kudasai (please wait).
